taxonomic_note: Current Kew/POWO accepts Nassella leucotricha; older Texas literature commonly uses Stipa leucotricha.
look_here_first: COOL-SEASON winter-green clump first: Texas wintergrass often greens during winter while warm-season grasses brown. At bloom in spring, the panicle is loose or somewhat narrowed with distinct long-awned individual spikelets, as the new Sam Kieschnick photo shows. Crucially, FOLLOW ONE mature floret to its ONE long, twisted and twice-bent awn attached to a hard lemma, then verify a long sharp hairy callus at the opposite base. The USDA example arrows show the callus, lemma and awn of ONE fruit. Nearby Aristida has THREE awn limbs from one lemma; cultivated Mexican feathergrass also has a single awn but a tiny blunt callus and thinner rolled foliage. New same-taxon actual Harms scaled photos show collar/sheath, spikelet flowers, mature one-awed hard fruit and empty glumes. The true ligule is a SHORT glabrous membranous structure often 0-1 mm and may appear absent. Do not mistake long collar hairs for the ligule or pale empty glumes for the hardened sharp fruit.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Hays — UT Plant Resources Center Flora of Purola Preserve, N. Hays County explicitly records Nassella leucotricha. Travis — Travis County environmental documentation explicitly records Texas wintergrass (Nassella leucotricha) in native grassland/woodland vegetation; Barton Creek Habitat Preserve research also lists it as a dominant herbaceous species in Travis County. Williamson — UT Plant Resources Center Vascular Plants of Williamson County provides a detailed treatment under the synonym Stipa leucotricha.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: No county occurrence inferred from statewide or ecoregion distribution alone.

best_field_traits: COOL SEASON: Texas wintergrass grows green and actively through fall, winter and early spring, sometimes when little bluestem and KR are tan; seasonal timing is support, not a stand-alone species ID.
PANICLE: loose open flowering branches bearing individual one-flowered spikelets, unlike Aristida's familiar three terminal awns and little bluestem's many short separate silky racemes.
FLORET: each narrow, hardened fertile lemma has ONE long twisted, usually twice-bent AWN (often ~40–90 mm); do not count awns from DIFFERENT spikelets.
SHARP SEED BASE: a long pointed, often hairy CALLUS forms the speargrass barb; handle dry seeds carefully and inspect under magnification.
CROWN/NECK: near the awn insertion, the mature lemma has a pale membranous apical crown/neck, commonly with a ring of hairs, visible with a strong hand lens.
GLUMES: two persistent pale, often oatlike bracts around the developing floret, roughly 10–21 mm in FNA; after fruit drops, empty whitish glumes may remain.
LEAF: rough dark-green narrow blades with short stiff whitish hairs, culm nodes usually somewhat hairy; leaf collar often has lateral tufts of short hairs.
DON'T CONFUSE: Mexican feathergrass (Nassella tenuissima) is also one-awned but has a very fine hairlike rolled blade, generally smaller/flimsier florets and a far SHORTER blunter callus.
Additional clue for field season: Texas wintergrass may form self-pollinating cleistogenous florets in basal leaf sheaths; these alone do not identify a sterile plant.
morphology_keys.joey_family_training: Poaceae family training: identify inflorescence architecture first, then inspect spikelets/glumes/lemma-palea/awns and ligule-collar-sheath characters.
morphology_keys.habit: Cool-season perennial tufted bunchgrass, often conspicuously green in winter in open native Central Texas grassland; can be up to 1.2 m tall in fruiting shoots.
morphology_keys.inflorescence: Open to sometimes rather contracted slender panicle, generally bearing well-spaced one-flowered spikelets rather than Aristida's trifid awn per lemma; FNA describes terminal panicles 5–55 cm with 1–4 spikelets on branchlets.
morphology_keys.fruit: Mature dry fruit enveloped by a hardened linear lemma terminating below in a pointed often hairy callus (~1–5.5 mm FNA); one rope-twisted twice-bent awn (~40–90 mm FNA, more variable across other Texas treatments) extends above a collar/crown. These sharp diaspores can penetrate skin, clothing and livestock tissue. Avoid handling without care.
morphology_keys.collars_and_ligules: Leaf blades rough from whitish bristles; sheaths may be hairy. Collars may show lateral short-hair tufts and brown/purple shading; membranous ligule often ~0.2–1.2 mm (FNA). Compare with broad Poaceae anatomical glossary if no macro.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Aristida (oldfield and purple threeawn): THREE terminal lemma awn branches from ONE floret, rather than Nassella leucotricha's SINGLE awn. Mexican feathergrass N. tenuissima: ALSO has ONE long awn, but tightly hairlike rolled leaves, much SMALLER fertile lemma (~1.8–3.6 mm versus N. leucotricha ~5.3–13 mm across major descriptions), and a very short blunt callus (~0.2–0.4 mm vs leucotricha usually >1 mm). Little bluestem: warm-season with many short silky separate racemes along upper leafy branches, not a loose wintergreen needlegrass panicle. Canada and Virginia wildrye: cool-season grasses too, but bear multiple awned spikelets clustered into more obvious spikes; inspect floret awn placement and entire inflorescence.

field_matrix.taxon: Purple / oldfield threeawn — Aristida purpurea / A. oligantha
field_matrix.where_to_look: Select one intact FERTILE LEMMA and count awns arising from that very same floret.
field_matrix.this_species: Texas wintergrass: ONE rope-twisted, often twice-bent, long awn attached to ONE hardened, sharp-callused lemma; loose winter/spring flowering panicle.
field_matrix.look_alike: Aristida: THREE spreading awn BRANCHES extend from ONE lemma; many threeawns are warm-season and share wiry grass habit.
field_matrix.quick_rule: One awn on a sharply pointed needlegrass lemma favors Nassella; three awn tips from one lemma points to Aristida. Detached awns without attachment cannot decide.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Inspect actual mature lemma, callus and leaf blade width with 1-mm scale.
field_matrix.this_species: Wintergrass has a larger floret/lemma (~5.3–13 mm depending treatment), longer sharp hairy callus (about 1.2–5.5 mm in Flora of North America), rough blades usually 1–3.6 mm wide, and a pale corona/neck.
field_matrix.look_alike: Mexican feathergrass is a dense soft fine-hairlike clump with extremely narrow tightly rolled leaves (often ≤0.5 mm), much smaller lemma (~1.8–3.6 mm) and short ~0.2–0.4 mm rather blunt callus; its awn can ALSO be very long.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Do not use ONE awn alone. A noticeably elongate sharp callus and larger lemma support N. leucotricha; tiny short blunt callus + filamentous leaf supports N. tenuissima.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Trace an attached flowering stalk and record whether the specimen was green through winter.
field_matrix.this_species: Cool-season perennial, open needlegrass panicle, one twisted awn per hard pointed fruit; basal photos show narrow rough green blades.
field_matrix.look_alike: Warm-season little bluestem repeatedly carries individual SHORT silky racemes at different upper leafy branch tips; fall bronze color is supporting only.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Wintergreen bunch with one-awned individual fruit and loose flowering panicle favors wintergrass; many separate upper short silky racemes favors little.

field_matrix.taxon: Canada / Virginia wildrye — Elymus canadensis / E. virginicus
field_matrix.where_to_look: Check whether spikelets crowd onto a single conspicuous terminal SPIKE (wheatlike) or form a branching open PANICLE.
field_matrix.this_species: Nassella has open/loose or narrow panicle of more isolated ONE-flowered spikelets and long single twisting awns on hard fruit.
field_matrix.look_alike: Elymus wildryes have multiple spikelets at successive axis nodes in terminal spikes; longer awns can give a bristly silhouette but the flowering architecture differs.
field_matrix.quick_rule: A conspicuous wheat/rye-like spike of multiple spikelets is not the loose individual-flowered Nassella panicle.

not_reliable_alone: Number of awns visible across the ENTIRE seedhead: count only those on one intact lemma.
Green winter growth, by itself; many other native cool-season grasses remain green.
Long awn length alone, since Mexican feathergrass also has a long awn.
Pale oatlike empty glumes when actual fruit has shed, without a same-plant mature floret.
Purple, gold or straw grass color or a graceful clump silhouette.
Detached long awn, or sharp fruit without intact glumes and stem, when source identity is uncertain.

visual_comparison.title: Texas wintergrass — real winter clump, spring flowering, twice-bent awn, sharp fruit and empty glumes
visual_comparison.subtitle: 12 credited panels including 6 Central Texas Bob Harms educational-use real photos of leaf sheath/collar, flowering, spikelet, mature awn and persistent glumes. His images are NOT Creative Commons. The same-voucher 0.5mm ligule and exact crown remain last-mile holds. visual_comparison.memory_rule: Start with cool-season green bunch, THEN open spring panicle; trace ONE attached mature floret. One long twice-bent twisted AWN and an elongated sharp hairy CALLUS support Texas wintergrass. THREE limbs from one lemma = Aristida. One awn alone does not exclude Mexican feathergrass.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Texas wintergrass — green tuft → panicle → scaled flowers → long one-awned fruit → empty glumes
steps: 1. In winter or early spring, FIND the actual green bunch like photo 1 (CC BY John Thomlinson). It is not unique enough to identify this grass alone.

2. At flowering, photograph a COMPLETE head from that same individual: photo 2 (CC BY Sam Kieschnick) shows narrow attached floral units and long threadlike awns among thin branches. Avoid guessing awn count from a whole head.

3. Select ONE mature FERTILE LEMMA, not an empty glume or another fruit: USDA image photo 3 has precise verified arrows for SHARP HAIRY CALLUS at its base, HARD LEMMA BODY and ONE rope-twisted awn above.
4. Compare Aristida: three terminal awn LIMBS depart from the SAME individual lemma. Other long awns in the photo may belong to other florets.
5. Compare Mexican feathergrass N. tenuissima: it also has one long awn, but the mature lemma and especially the CALLUS are substantially smaller/blunter; photograph and measure actual adult fruits.

6. When safe, use hand lens to inspect 0.2–1.2 mm SHORT membranous ligule, 0.75–2 mm pale flared crown/neck beneath awn, and 1–5.5 mm sharp often hairy callus (Flora of North America treatment, individual measured specimens vary). All still lack verified high-resolution same-plant local teaching photos.

Harms photos 7–9: examine a real blade/sheath junction then attached spring floral spikelets and pale glumes. True 0–1mm membrane needs a genuine 10–20× close-up: these gross pictures do not prove the ligule-tip pixels.
Harms photos 10–11 show a ONE-awed hardened lemma with a long twice-bent/twisted awn and nearby physical scale; still collect a same-specimen measured crown and sharp basal callus macro.
Harms photo 12 shows EMPTY glumes after hardened seed-bearing unit drops. Crew should distinguish empty glumes on stalk from USDA image 3: a detached hard seed-bearing lemma plus sharp basal callus.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Visible gross photos: winter-active bunch -> attached often loose spring flowering head. first_field_sequence: Look for native Texas wintergrass active green in late fall to early spring as a cool-season bunch.

diagnostic_species_finalization_20261024.look_here_first: Texas wintergrass: winter-active perennial tuft, then a spring flowering culm bearing solitary one-flowered spikelets. Confirm ONE long twisted twice-bent awn on ONE hardened lemma, a sharp hairy basal callus and a pale distal crown. Neither winter greenness nor one loose awn alone establishes species.
crew_steps: 1. Follow the rooted tuft to an attached panicle. FNA describes a cespitose perennial with culms 33–120 cm; Kew gives 20–50 cm. Growth and height support, but do not prove, identification.

2. Unfold the TRUE inner blade/sheath junction: ligule is a glabrous truncate MEMBRANE, FNA 0.2–1.2 mm and Kew 0.4–0.7 mm. Lateral collar hair tufts (FNA 0.5–1 mm) are separate. Photograph at 10–20× with 0.5-mm ruler.
3. Photograph the intact spring panicle. FNA terminal panicles 5–55 cm, branches 3–7 cm with 1–4 spikelets; Kew describes a contracted ~15 cm panicle. Head silhouette varies.

4. At 10–20× dissect ONE 1-flowered mature spikelet. Two pale persistent GLUMES enclose the hardened fertile lemma: FNA glumes 10–21 mm and 3–5-veined; Kew lower 10–17 mm, 3-veined and upper 10–16 mm, 3(–5)-veined. Backlight veins and measure both glumes independently.

5. Identify the hard, tightly inrolled fertile LEMMA (Kew body 5.3–5.7 mm) and mostly concealed narrow palea. FNA's 6.5–13 mm figure describes the whole FLORET, not the isolated lemma body; do not conflate the units.
6. Rotate the floret under 20–40×: its sharp hairy basal CALLUS measures FNA 1–5.5 mm or Kew 1.2–3.3 mm. The distal pale CROWN/CORONA is separate, FNA 0.75–2 mm or Kew 1.5–2.5 mm.

7. Trace the single lemma AWN from insertion to tip with a ruler: twisted column and usually two bends; FNA 40–90 mm, Kew 50–60 mm (twisted column 20–30 mm). Do not count awns from adjacent florets as multiple awns on one lemma.

8. Compare one mature floret at the SAME scale. Aristida oligantha/purpurea have THREE awn limbs from one lemma; Mexican feathergrass Nassella tenuissima also has one awn but much finer rolled leaves and a much shorter blunter callus. If the callus and crown are not resolved, record needlegrass candidate, not 100% confirmation.

measured_diagnostic_key.growth: Cespitose perennial, culms FNA 33–120 cm / Kew 20–50 cm; no claim of roots seen in existing photos.
measured_diagnostic_key.ligule_collar: TRUE glabrous truncate membrane FNA 0.2–1.2 mm / Kew 0.4–0.7 mm; lateral collar hairs FNA 0.5–1 mm, NOT ligule.
measured_diagnostic_key.panicle: FNA 5–55 cm, branchlets 3–7 cm / Kew contracted ~15 cm by 1–3 cm.
measured_diagnostic_key.spikelet: One fertile floret; Kew 10–17 mm spikelet; FNA 10–21 mm glumes; avoid equating spikelet and isolated lemma lengths.
measured_diagnostic_key.lower_glume: Kew 10–17 mm, 3 veins; FNA paired glumes 10–21 mm, 3–5 veins.
measured_diagnostic_key.upper_glume: Kew 10–16 mm, 3(–5) veins; persistent after fruit shedding.
measured_diagnostic_key.fertile_lemma: Kew hardened inrolled body 5.3–5.7 mm; FNA floret 6.5–13 mm (different measurement unit).
measured_diagnostic_key.callus: Sharp hairy basal attachment FNA 1–5.5 mm / Kew 1.2–3.3 mm.
measured_diagnostic_key.crown: Pale membranous apical corona FNA 0.75–2 mm / Kew 1.5–2.5 mm.
measured_diagnostic_key.awn: One lemma awn, twice bent and twisted; FNA 40–90 mm / Kew 50–60 mm; Kew twisted column 20–30 mm.

diagnostic_species_finalization_20261024.local_lookalikes: Aristida oligantha/purpurea: THREE awn limbs from ONE lemma; N. tenuissima: also ONE awn, but very fine rolled blades and short blunt callus; Elymus: terminal spike of grouped spikelets; Schizachyrium scoparium: separate silky upper racemes and paired spikelet structure. Do not rely on green winter habit alone.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST
field_id_short_tiles.short: Winter-green bunch; in spring, follow ONE awned floret to a pointed seed base
field_id_short_tiles.details: Texas wintergrass is a cool-season perennial tuft, often green while warm-season bluestems are dormant. Follow an attached spring panicle to ONE mature single-flowered spikelet. One long twisted and often twice-bent awn plus an elongated sharp callus support the ID; winter color alone cannot certify the species. Existing winter-tuft and flowering panels show useful gross traits, not a connected rooted specimen.
field_id_short_tiles.status: FIELD-READY GROSS CUE; NEEDS SAME-PLANT ROOTED SPRING MATERIAL

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · OPEN THE COLLAR
field_id_short_tiles.short: True membrane ~0.2–1.2 mm; side hairs are NOT the ligule
field_id_short_tiles.details: Open a fresh blade–sheath junction and inspect the very short glabrous truncate membranous ligule. Flora of North America reports ~0.2–1.2 mm (Kew ~0.4–0.7 mm), while adjacent collar hair tufts may reach ~0.5–1 mm. Photograph membrane and hairs separately at 10–20× with 0.5-mm scale. The archived sheath photo does not prove an accurately measured membrane.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · CHECK THE ONE-FLOWERED SPIKELET
field_id_short_tiles.short: Two persistent pale glumes ~10–21 mm (FNA); not the hardened seed-bearing lemma
field_id_short_tiles.details: In a fresh spring spikelet identify the paired pale 3–5-veined glumes enclosing ONE fertile floret. Flora of North America describes glumes ~10–21 mm; Kew gives lower ~10–17 mm and upper ~10–16 mm. When the ripe floret sheds, empty glumes can remain attached (panel 12). Measure the attached glumes and do not mistake an empty pair for a detached seed-bearing lemma.
field_id_short_tiles.status: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — MEASURED GLUMES ON ONE ATTACHED SPIKELET

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · FOLLOW THE HARD LEMMA TO ITS CALLUS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Hard lemma ~5.3–5.7 mm (Kew); basal sharp hairy callus ~1–5.5 mm (FNA)
field_id_short_tiles.details: A mature fruit has a hardened rolled fertile lemma, a sharp often hairy basal callus and a pale apical crown. Kew reports a ~5.3–5.7 mm lemma body; FNA's ~6.5–13 mm floret figure is a DIFFERENT measurement, not a contradiction to erase. Callus ranges ~1–5.5 mm (FNA) and crown ~0.75–2 mm (FNA). Panels show actual hard fruit, but same-voucher calibrated callus and crown views remain needed.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · COUNT THE AWNS ON ONE LEMMA
field_id_short_tiles.short: ONE twisted, usually twice-bent awn ~40–90 mm (FNA); not three
field_id_short_tiles.details: Trace the long awn from the actual hardened lemma tip: FNA gives ~40–90 mm and Kew ~50–60 mm. Do not count neighboring awns from different spikelets as branches of one awn. The sharp basal callus and apical pale crown should be photographed at the same time as the awn insertion; existing scaled Bob Harms photos show important gross parts but do not close every same-specimen microscopic hold.
field_id_short_tiles.status: FIELD-READY SINGLE-AWN CLUE; ATTACHMENT/CROWN SCALE GAP

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · SEPARATE THREEAWNS AND FEATHERGRASS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Aristida has THREE awn limbs per lemma; Mexican feathergrass also has ONE but a tiny blunt callus
field_id_short_tiles.details: Purple/oldfield threeawn (Aristida purpurea / A. oligantha) has three awn limbs arising from ONE lemma, unlike Texas wintergrass. Mexican feathergrass (Nassella tenuissima) ALSO has one long awn, but much finer tightly rolled leaves, smaller mature lemma and a short ~0.2–0.4 mm relatively blunt callus. Compare ripe fruits at the SAME scale. Little bluestem has multiple short silky racemes; wildryes form terminal spikes rather than this loose panicle.
field_id_short_tiles.status: FIELD-READY LOOK-ALIKES; MATCHED FRUIT MICROPHOTOS MISSING
